subproblem.title: Lusin's theorem for ℝ^N-valued Borel maps on a set of finite μ-measure
subproblem.statement: Let N ∈ ℕ, let μ be a measure on the Borel σ-algebra of ℝ^N (= EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N)); no local finiteness is assumed. Let f : ℝ^N → ℝ^N be Borel measurable, let A ⊆ ℝ^N be a Borel set with μ(A) < ∞, and let ε ∈ (0, ∞]. Then there is a closed set C ⊆ ℝ^N with C ⊆ A, μ(A ∖ C) < ε, and f continuous on C (i.e. the restriction f|C is continuous).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Rn N)) (f : Rn N → Rn N) (A : Set (Rn N)), Measurable f → MeasurableSet A → μ A ≠ ∞ → ∀ ε : ℝ≥0∞, 0 < ε → ∃ C ⊆ A, IsClosed C ∧ μ (A \ C) < ε ∧ ContinuousOn f C
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. This is step 5 of the parent proof: Lusin's theorem applied coordinatewise to the finite Borel measure μ⌞A.
- Lusin's theorem: Simon Ch. 1, Theorem 1.17, chapter-01.txt lines 346–372. For real-valued functions it is formalized as SimonGMT Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.exists_isClosed_continuousOn_of_measurable in Poincare/SimonGMT/Chapter01/Lusin.lean. That module is not in the import closure of GMT.Ch03.Submission, so add `import Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.Lusin`.
- Regularity: finite Borel measures on metric spaces are closed-inner-regular (Simon Ch. 1, Theorem 1.15(2), chapter-01.txt lines 274–343).
- Generalizations of the parent argument: A is an arbitrary Borel set of finite measure and f an arbitrary Borel map. An extra closed set F is intersected in so that N = 0 needs no separate case.

1. The restricted measure. Let ρ := μ⌞A, i.e. ρ(S) := μ(S ∩ A) for Borel S. Then ρ(ℝ^N) = μ(A) < ∞, so ρ is a finite Borel measure on the metric space ℝ^N. For every Borel S ⊆ A, ρ(S) = μ(S).
2. Closed inner regularity of ρ. For every Borel S and every δ > 0 there is a closed F ⊆ S with ρ(S ∖ F) < δ. This is Simon Ch. 1, Theorem 1.15(2) for the finite measure ρ: in a metric space every closed set is a countable intersection of open sets. In Mathlib, ρ is weakly regular (Measure.WeaklyRegular.of_pseudoMetrizableSpace_of_isFiniteMeasure, with IsFiniteMeasure ρ from isFiniteMeasure_restrict), and MeasurableSet.exists_isClosed_sdiff_lt gives F.
3. Choice of δ. Since ε > 0, choose a real δ > 0 with (N + 1)·δ < ε. If ε = ∞, any δ > 0 works. Otherwise take δ := ε/(2(N + 1)). (Mathlib ENNReal.exists_pos_mul_lt gives δ with δ·(N + 1) < ε.)
4. A closed subset of A. By step 2 with S = A, there is a closed F ⊆ A with ρ(A ∖ F) < δ.
5. Coordinates. For i = 1, …, N let f^i(x) := f(x)_i be the i-th coordinate. f^i : ℝ^N → ℝ is Borel, as the composition of f with the continuous coordinate projection (EuclideanSpace.proj i). Apply Lusin's theorem for real functions to ρ, the Borel set A with ρ(A) < ∞, the function f^i and the tolerance δ. Its regularity hypothesis is exactly step 2. This gives a closed C_i ⊆ A with ρ(A ∖ C_i) < δ such that f^i is continuous on C_i.
6. Definition of C. Put C := F ∩ C_1 ∩ … ∩ C_N. C is closed as a finite intersection of closed sets, and C ⊆ F ⊆ A. When N = 0 there are no C_i and C = F; intersecting with F guarantees C ⊆ A in all cases.
7. Measure estimate. If x ∈ A ∖ C, then x ∉ F or x ∉ C_i for some i, so A ∖ C ⊆ (A ∖ F) ∪ ⋃_{i=1}^N (A ∖ C_i). All of these are Borel subsets of A, so by step 1 and subadditivity
 μ(A ∖ C) = ρ(A ∖ C) ≤ ρ(A ∖ F) + Σ_{i=1}^N ρ(A ∖ C_i) < δ + N·δ = (N + 1)·δ < ε.
8. Continuity. Each f^i is continuous on C, since C ⊆ C_i and f^i is continuous on C_i. The coordinate map z ↦ (z_1, …, z_N) is a linear homeomorphism from ℝ^N onto ℝ^{Fin N} (Mathlib EuclideanSpace.equiv). A map into a finite product is continuous on C iff each coordinate is (continuousOn_pi). So x ↦ (f^1(x), …, f^N(x)) is continuous on C, and composing with the inverse homeomorphism shows that f is continuous on C. ∎
proof_key_steps: ρ := μ⌞A is a finite Borel measure on a metric space, so every Borel set contains a closed set of nearly full ρ-measure.
Fix δ > 0 with (N+1)δ < ε. Take a closed F ⊆ A with ρ(A∖F) < δ, and by real Lusin closed C_i ⊆ A with ρ(A∖C_i) < δ and f^i continuous on C_i.
C := F ∩ C_1 ∩ … ∩ C_N is closed, C ⊆ A, and μ(A∖C) = ρ(A∖C) ≤ ρ(A∖F) + Σ_i ρ(A∖C_i) < (N+1)δ < ε.
Every coordinate of f is continuous on C, so f is continuous on C.

audit.reason: The finite restriction μ⌞A supplies weak regularity without assuming local finiteness of μ. Scalar Lusin applies to every coordinate; intersecting with the additional closed F handles N = 0. Subadditivity and coordinate continuity prove the exact stated conclusion.
